title: Demystifying Group Relative Policy Optimization: Its Policy Gradient is a U-Statistic
data_curation: Not a focus of this paper. Empirical validation uses a synthetic arithmetic dataset of 500 medium-difficulty integer problems uniformly drawn from five categories (two/three-step add-subtract, single-step multiplication, integer division, parenthesized add-subtract) with binary correctness rewards, plus the public math reasoning benchmarks GSM8K and MATH for the group-size experiments. No de-duplication, filtering, or scaling of training data is discussed.
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. GRPO is analyzed in isolation as a single-stage RLVR post-training loop (Algorithm 1/2: sample prompts, generate G outputs each, compute group-relative advantages, SGD update). No pretrain->SFT->preference staging, warmup/anneal schedule, self-play loop, or cross-stage data mixing is considered.
method: The core contribution shows GRPO's policy-gradient estimator is a second-order U-statistic (Lemma 1). A meta-algorithm unifies REINFORCE, A2C, and GRPO, differing only in the baseline subtracted from reward Z: zero, the true value function (oracle), or the leave-one-out group mean (GRPO). GRPO thus replaces the critic by sampling G outputs per prompt. Hoeffding decomposition splits the U-statistic into a first-order term equal to the oracle gradient and a G^-2 degenerate residual, yielding MSE bounds (Theorem 2, Prop. 3), an oracle property (MSE -> oracle as G->inf, Cor. 4), and optimality (minimizes MSE among prompt-only baselines, strictly beating vanilla REINFORCE, Cor. 5). For policy optimization, Lemma 6 bounds the suboptimality gap under L-smoothness, PL, and constant or 1/i learning rates, giving a scaling law (Theorem 7): the bound c1/B + c2/(BG) + c3/(BG^2) is minimized by a universal group size G* = sqrt(c3/c1), independent of budget and iterations. Theorem 8 gives consistency and a chi-squared-mixture asymptotic distribution for the gap without parameter identifiability (overparameterized regime); Corollaries 9/10 extend oracle/optimality to the learned policy. Appendix A extends this to production GRPO with reward standardization, token-level importance sampling, and a Schulman K3 KL penalty, confirming the objective becomes an arcsin transform of expected reward.
eval_metrics: Two experiments validate the theory. (1) Gradient MSE (Figure 4): on a synthetic 500-question arithmetic set, with target policies Qwen2.5-0.5B Base/Instruct/ICL and G in {4,8,16,32,64}, Monte-Carlo MSE shows vanilla (REINFORCE) largest, GRPO-type strictly smaller, and already close to the oracle at G>=8, nearly indistinguishable at G=32,64; MSE also drops with stronger models. (2) Optimal group size: on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B Instruct (N=BG=1024, G in {4,...,128}, 5 runs, checkpoints n in {200,...,800}), test accuracy peaks at G*=32 across steps except n=200, confirming universality over iterations. On MATH with Qwen2.5-Math-7B (N in {1024,2048,4096}, single run), accuracy is about 0.77 with best G mostly 64, rising to 128 at the largest budget, suggesting larger models favor larger G. Metrics are gradient MSE (95% CIs) and test accuracy (% correctly solved).
key_results: GRPO's gradient MSE is strictly below vanilla REINFORCE and matches the oracle (true-critic) estimator for G>=8 (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Figure 4). The optimal per-prompt group size is universal: G*=32 on GSM8K (Qwen2.5-1.5B, N=1024) across iterations and about 64 on MATH (Qwen2.5-Math-7B), given analytically by G*=sqrt(c3/c1).
evolution_note: Builds on DeepSeekMath/DeepSeek-R1's GRPO (2024-2025) and classical U-statistics (Hoeffding 1948), reacting to the theoretical gap left by RLVR works such as Davis & Recht and Pang & Jin. In the 2026 GRPO-variant boom, it supplies the first unified finite-sample and asymptotic theory plus a budget-independent group-size scaling law, enabling principled hyperparameter selection for the flood of critic-free RLVR algorithms.
